video_title: Why China Is Going After Anthropic
transcript: Tom Reed: Today I’m speaking with Julian  Gewirtz. Julian is a historian, poet,   former director for China affairs in the NSC  [National Security Council] under Biden, and   more recently also a blogger. Of all the things  that I’ve learned from reading Julian’s work,   perhaps my favourite is that much of the credit  we all usually give to Deng Xiaoping for the   reform of China’s economy should instead  be redirected towards the comparatively   uncelebrated former Chinese Premier Zhao Ziyang.  Julian, thank you for coming on the show. Julian Gewirtz: Thanks, Tom.  It’s great to be with you. Tom Reed: So, Julian, I have a bunch  of not-so-hidden agendas for speaking   to you. Above all, I want to understand:  what on Earth do you think Xi Jinping’s   model of Dario Amodei is? What do  you think he thinks this guy wants? Julian Gewirtz: Well, honestly, I don’t think we  have to speculate, because to a stunning degree,   Beijing has been on the record going after  Anthropic. In the history of sort of US–China   relations, it’s hard for me to think of another  example of an American company that Beijing has   taken on so repeatedly and so directly.  There have been a series of state media   commentaries about it. There was one ahead  of Xi Jinping coming to the United States   that I found really striking, and  I wrote a little bit about it, but   the headline was “Anthropic has  contracted the American disease.” Now, what does that mean? The core argument  was basically that this is a company that   says whatever, but is actually all about  preserving so-called technological hegemony   for the United States. And crucially, we often  think about these different AI companies,   the different model companies, as very  differentiated actors in our system.   We know that many of them don’t like each  other and that they’re competing intensely,   and all of those sort of things that define  what it feels like to be in this space. Beijing said Anthropic is literally “a monster  bred by the American path” — saying, like,   all of this, all of these different firms,  this is all part of one big thing. And that   big thing is the United States trying to dominate  globally and trying to keep China behind. And   they have been going at Anthropic hardest,  but they don’t, I think, see it as somehow   separate or outside of a mainstream in the  United States, but very much a part of it. And it’s just maybe worth driving home the  upshot of that, which is that for Beijing,   it appears that a lot of the distinctions or  differences in views among American tech titans   and American AI companies matter  less than what they represent to   China, which is the project of  American power, in their eyes. Tom Reed: Sometimes I get confused  by Dario’s comms on China, because   sometimes it sounds like he’s calling for  we really need to cooperate with them;   sometimes it sounds like what he’s calling  for looks a little bit less like cooperation. Dario, famously, I think he  only has one direct report,   which is his chief of staff. But let’s imagine  you were his second-ever direct report,   and he’d hired you specifically as his China  comms person. What would you tell him to say?   How should he be talking about China differently  in a way that actually increases the chance of   them taking his calls seriously, rather than as  a call for slowing China down compared to the US? Julian Gewirtz: Well, I guess, honestly, I don’t  think it’s very likely that Beijing can somehow   be disabused of the notion that the United States  wants a significant lead in AI over China. And I   don’t think that messaging from any particular  executive is going to be the key thing there. I mean, let’s just step back for a second and  say we’re in a moment where the president of the   United States has said, “No slowdown. AI risk  is not something I want to take seriously.” Tom Reed: “It’s a hoax.” Julian Gewirtz: Sure. And where the  secretary of the Treasury has said,   “There’s no day after tomorrow if China wins  at this.” To the point I was just making,   I actually don’t think that they see  the rhetoric or comms of one CEO,   Dario or otherwise, as the thing  that could shift their view. My own strong view is that the most  important thing that could cause Beijing   to shift its current approach to AI safety  is their own domestic sense of the risks.   The second most important thing is if they  were to see the United States actually   doing AI regulation and taking AI safety  seriously — doing basically what we would   call a “costly signal,” the kind of thing that  we’re doing because we care about these risks,   and that also has the benefit of signalling  to Beijing, like, “Hey, these guys are serious   about this.” Those two things are far more  important, I think, than a shift in comms. I will say I do think that there is a difference  between the United States wanting to compete   and have a lead, and a narrative of total  supremacy, permanent dominance. So the language,   I think, that is least helpful toward getting  Beijing there is the language that suggests   that what the United States wants here is not  just a lead, but total kind of what we would call   “primacy.” And there is a distinction there, and  I think it is relevant, but all part of a puzzle. Tom Reed: So the idea being that a  precondition for China taking any   of the US’s apparent AI safety  concerns seriously would be:   actually regulate AI domestically.  Otherwise it just looks like it’s all talk. Julian Gewirtz: Yeah. And obviously that gets  us right into the core question of tradeoffs   around regulating at home to preserve our edge,  and regulating at home with the risk of losing   our edge over China. But there, my friend and  collaborator Matt Sheehan has a really good point,   which is that Beijing has itself done some AI  regulation at home — not sort of frontier AI risk,   but they have deepfake and AI-generated  content labelling requirements. They   have regulations on chatbots, particularly  for minors. They’ve done some stuff there. And of course we don’t see that as condemning  them to be in second place necessarily. In fact,   they’re doing all that and we’re still  very worried about them catching up to us. So I think there’s a bit of a fallacy embedded  in the idea that any AI regulation is at odds— Tom Reed: Going to lose us the whole race. Julian Gewirtz: Exactly. Now, pacing is a  separate question, because that is explicitly   about the speed of frontier development. But  regulation is a lot more than just pacing. Tom Reed: How do you think the  Chinese government would react   to a homegrown version of  the Hugging Face incident? Julian Gewirtz: Now, in China, I think  an incident like that would be seen as   a cybersecurity incident first and foremost.  And the thing to remember in China is that   while the AI regulatory space, and particularly  the frontier AI regulatory space, is very much   still coming together — and we’ll talk about  that, I’m sure — the cybersecurity structures   have been in place for a while, and this is a  top kind of regime security issue for Beijing. So I think they’d treat it that way. They do have  certain kind of notification requirements where I   think the central government could potentially  become aware of it pretty quickly. But the most   important thing that I think we have to stress  is that at every layer, the incentives in that   system are not to disclose more information,  and certainly not to disclose it publicly. So the most remarkable thing, as we  imagine what a kind of Hugging Face,   OpenAI-style incident in China  would look like, is the public,   I don’t think, would know about  it. We might never know about it. And I think that’s part of the reason why  there’s so much concern as we think about these   issues. Because in the Chinese political system,  whistleblower protections, shall we say, are not   something that gets treated with much seriousness.  The famous Chinese whistleblowers are people like   the doctor in Wuhan who warned about the spread  of COVID and was punished for that years ago. So I think anyone at a firm — whether  an executive wanting to report up the   chain or a whistleblower kind of  considering whether to make their   concerns known — would be weighing the  risk of serious kind of smackdown by   the government against the safety risks. And  so that’s a pretty challenging place to be. Tom Reed: Interesting. Do you think the  government would be fully informed of   what happened, or do you think the labs  themselves would also be incentivised   and capable of hiding such an incident  if they became aware of it? I’m just   trying to understand exactly who would  know if something like this happened. Julian Gewirtz: Well, in an incident like  that, where what happened fully escaped the   lab’s control and was a third-party website,  I think presumably the government would find   out that something had occurred, at least  via the third-party website. And if there   was an investigation, I think some of the  labs might be more forthcoming than others. And there is a small chance you could imagine  that if they felt they really kind of handled   it — and/or if it became publicly known  that there had been some sort of hack of   this third-party website for other reasons  that were visible — I think you could then   imagine them doing a very limited kind of  disclosure, saying, “There was a problem,   we found out about it, we solved it,  everything is good, proceed accordingly.” I think the biggest policy question in  Beijing in that kind of moment would be:   would something like that trigger what they would  call a “broader rectification campaign,” meaning   an effort to bring greater control from the  central authorities over this area? And that,   I think, is possible. But again, it would  likely be in a context without the kind of   public disclosure that eventually marked the  OpenAI Hugging Face incident. And crucially,   that METR report — the things that have  brought a bit more public confidence   back to thinking that at least third-party  evaluators have the capacity to inform the   public about this — I think highly unlikely  in the Chinese case that that would happen. Tom Reed: Is there a particular flavour  of near-term AI incident that you think   would be more likely to cause something  like a broader rectification campaign?   What I’m trying to think of is: are there  some kinds of ways that AI could go rogue   that would be more worrying to the CCP  [Chinese Communist Party] than others,   or that might encourage them to view things  as not just any other familiar cyber incident? Julian Gewirtz: We have to start with  the reality of what China is and what   the Chinese Communist Party cares about,  as opposed to kind of working backwards   from the place we think they need to get  in order to accomplish our broader goals. And I say that because the number one concern  is regime security, regime stability — what they   call political security and social stability.  So the kinds of risks that I think are most   likely to cause them to recalibrate some of their  current approach to the AI sector are really in   that domain. They do want to avoid risks to regime  security, also sort of major economic disruptions.   So from that perspective, I think as we consider  the kinds of scenarios that might unfold,   it’s really the ones that are in that  core political and regime security space. And as your listeners well know, there are those  risks — and in fact, control over information,   particularly information about the  government, about the Communist Party,   access to a very carefully controlled cyber  and information ecosystem: that is the kind   of thing that we can imagine these new tools, new  technologies disrupting, either inadvertently via   loss of control by a company, or deliberately.  And I think the deliberate piece of this is a   big element to just bring in, because candidly,  as I have seen the Chinese AI discourse evolve,   there is increasing attention to what  they call “extreme loss-of-control risks.” But we have to remember that when they use  that phrase, “loss of control,” they don’t   simply mean it in the way that a lot of AI  safety folks here mean it — loss of human   control over AI systems — but also as the  loss of political control linked to AI more   generally. And so when we think of deliberate  hacking, deliberate dissemination of information   that the government doesn’t want spread,  those are all the kind of risks, I think,   that are likely in the first instance  to make them really start to reconsider. And, sorry, maybe just one last thing, but  there was recently this vulnerability exposed— Tom Reed: This is the hack of WeChat? Julian Gewirtz: Yeah, exactly.  The vulnerability in WeChat,   which is the sort of One App  to Rule Them All in China. Tom Reed: So just to clarify for our audience:  this was a hack of WeChat that was disclosed   by a group that had used AI to find the  vulnerability. They’d found a vulnerability,   but they disclosed it responsibly. But we  have no idea exactly how the government   sort of processed this information. We just know  that it happened and they would be aware of it. Julian Gewirtz: Right. And sort of in line  with what we were just saying a second ago,   the response of Tencent, the company  that created WeChat, was to say,   “We patched the vulnerability.” But the shoe that  never dropped publicly was how the government saw   that and what kind of conversations  about the vulnerability there were. But there was just one other thing which I should  have said in the prior set of comments, which is:   the US factor here is major. And I think in a  way, the most significant event in shaping the   evolution of Beijing’s thinking about AI risks  over the course of the past year or so is Mythos   — and the kind of sense that the United States is  gaining extraordinary capabilities in cyber. And   that that is motivating a set of counter-responses  that we have very little visibility into, but   that they see as part of the AI risk conversation  centrally. And whenever they talk about AI risk at   the government level or the party level, they talk  about the United States as one of the threats. Tom Reed: It’s like the main  risk for them is US primacy   through AI advantages or something like that? Julian Gewirtz: I still think loss of political  control, political security, is number one. But a   very close second is the US dimension, exactly  as you say. And crucially, they’re connected. Tom Reed: And how do we know that Mythos  was this sort of wake-up call for them?   I’ve heard this before, but how is it that  we know this is the case? They’ve not said,   “Oh, this was a wakeup call for us.” Are there  signs that Mythos shifted things for the CCP? Julian Gewirtz: No, I don’t think any  government would call a press conference   and say, “We’re really freaked out about  this.” But no, there are a few things. First, there are indications in official  statements where they have quite directly invoked   it. So they have spoken about it a little bit.  They don’t say, “We’ve turned up the alarm to   the highest level,” but they acknowledge  the reality of it, and they acknowledge it   as something that could pose a kind of security  set of challenges for China. And then second,   in track II dialogues and other  settings where there’s communication,   it’s been quite clear that this is something  that has reverberated profoundly in their system. And in general, to go back to that initial  point of starting from what China is and   what the party cares about, their concern about  American cyber capabilities and all the rest has   been a huge issue for well over a decade. Xi  Jinping has spoken about this frequently over   the years. So they are primed to see that as  a threat vector of the greatest significance. Tom Reed: Can I force you to  make a guess about something? Julian Gewirtz: Sure. You’re not going to  necessarily be able to force me, but you can try. Tom Reed: I could try, I could try. And yeah,  to clarify for our audience, I should say,   if you hadn’t heard about this: there  was a report released by Anthropic   where they discussed that requests from users to  Kimi models or models from DeepSeek were being   rerouted to Claude. And some of these  even included requests from, I think,   a PLA [People’s Liberation Army] official, even  in one instance. So really sensitive things that   people thought they were using a Chinese model  for, but was in fact being sent to Claude. What I’d love to know is: what do you think the  CCP officials who spoke to the CEOs of Moonshot   and DeepSeek about the data leaks to Claude,  what do you think that conversation was about? Julian Gewirtz: So the first thing I’d say is:   I wonder at what level of technical  sophistication that conversation happens,   because there’s a version of that conversation —  in our idealised version of, generally, globally,   how governments and private sector should interact  — that could be pretty technically sophisticated.   But I think it’s fairly unlikely that that was  the only kind of conversation that happened. I think it’s more likely that there was  a conversation about this — maybe that   did occur at a technical level, or they sent  in people from the Cyberspace Administration   or one of the real AI technical bodies  that does exist to understand how this   happened. But the political dimensions  of that — the idea that it embarrassed   China and embarrassed these companies — had  to have been front and centre. And that’s   the kind of thing that would probably  happen somewhat distinct from the more   technical conversation about what was actually  revealed and how did that actually happen. I think we all had the reaction reading  the Anthropic report that, like, first,   this is crazy. And it is a reminder  of how the incredibly fast-moving   Chinese efforts to catch up have led to a  degree, in some areas, of sloppiness that is   certainly not what a perfectly centrally planned  version of an AI race from Beijing’s perspective   would look like. And it is embarrassing.  I mean, it’s deeply embarrassing for them. And the broader point about distillation  and dependence on American models, though:   we were sort of talking just a second ago  about some political dimensions of that   conversation. It’s important to underscore  that Beijing’s line on distillation is not,   “It doesn’t happen, and how dare you.” It is  precisely, actually, “This is normal practice --” Tom Reed: Fair game. Yeah. Julian Gewirtz: “-- the United  States is trying to twist this   into something it’s not,” et cetera, et cetera. And I was also quite struck  that they connected that report   to when Dario came out with the call to pace the  frontier, and some of the China language there. One of the core points I always make about  China is that they connect dots in our system   that we may not connect ourselves. And candidly,  I think we do the same sometimes in their system;   we can come back to that. But they connected,  in very official, authoritative state media,   that report that we were just talking  about — including those really embarrassing   disclosures — with the calls to pace the frontier,  which included language about the need for the   US to stay ahead of China. They said, “See,  these are all part of the same initiative,   the same effort to make Chinese AI look  bad and keep the United States number one.” And candidly, I don’t think too many people in  the United States connected those. I’m not even   sure that Anthropic necessarily meant them  as part of some kind of coordinated thing.   I don’t know. But they saw it that way, and  it’s just a reminder of that core dynamic. Tom Reed: Yeah, that makes sense. Tom Reed: So it’s still deeply unclear how either  the US government or the Chinese government might   relate to a very rapid increase in AI  capabilities. How do you think about   the difference between how the American labs  versus the Chinese AI labs think about AI risk? Julian Gewirtz: It’s such an important question,  because that distinction in each country between   the governments and the labs is actually something  that can sometimes get overlooked by either   player. China often talks about the United States  ecosystem as just one monolithic thing. Obviously,   Americans often sometimes talk about  the Chinese ecosystem in the same way. And over the summer, my friend Dan Wang and I  wrote an essay in The New York Times that was   arguing essentially that we needed to focus more  on the competition for influence and bargaining   and dynamics within the United States and  China respectively than we do currently,   where the focus is largely on the  race between the two. And obviously   that’s become pretty salient in the  months since we wrote about that,   which was right around the time of the  US government and Anthropic dispute. I guess what I would say there is, to my mind, the  key difference is that the American labs — some of   them, at least — have a demonstrated track  record of taking safety somewhat seriously   and doing certain things to disclose to the  public, and to even in some cases constrain   their own racing forward. I think it’s nowhere  near what many of us would like to see, but   there is something of a track record there. And  candidly, we don’t have that on the Chinese side. I think when people talk about these questions  of where is the risk greater these days,   the US government certainly doesn’t seem  like it’s being particularly responsible.   But I think there is reason to say that some  of the American labs, at least, have behaved in   a way that is a little bit more attuned to the  safety concerns than some of the Chinese labs. Tom Reed: Do you never entertain cynicism — like,   cynicism toward the American  labs? Like, you take this— Julian Gewirtz: Do I? Absolutely. Tom Reed: Yeah. But why doesn’t that  make you more bearish? Or what gives   you the confidence that it’s not just show?  I have this opinion too, for what it’s worth. Julian Gewirtz: Yeah. I mean, I guess what  I’d say is I’m not terribly optimistic here.   I don’t want to convey the wrong impression  that I think somehow the American labs are   highly responsible stewards of the fate of  human civilisation. But I do think that the   incentives that they have had, at least so  far, to disclose incidents — very low bar,   not a bar that the Chinese labs have cleared.  So actually, I would frame this less as all   the things that we know they need to be  doing and are not doing, and just look   at the lowest possible bar of disclosure  — and that’s one fundamental difference. And so I think in both countries, the question of  how the relationship between government regulation   and lab self-regulation plays out is a huge  part of everything that we’re discussing today.   It’s going to play out differently in these two  countries. This is not going to be symmetrical,   for very obvious reasons. But if  we’re just looking at the labs,   some of those asymmetries, I think,  aren’t all a bad story for America. Tom Reed: Have you ever had the chance  to speak to people at Chinese AI labs? Julian Gewirtz: Yeah, to some. I mean, look,   I’m a former US government official. I’m not  somebody who I think Chinese labs have a— Tom Reed: Speak candidly to. Julian Gewirtz: Well, I don’t know about that.  I think the most striking conversations that   I’ve had with folks at Chinese labs were around  the kind of early wave of discussion of pacing,   sort of when the lab employees’  letter came out in the United States. And I asked a bunch of these folks how they  interpreted that. And one person said to me,   in a comment that I found very  striking, “The United States has   been pacing the frontier for China for  years. So we don’t see this as really   anything new about us. And we don’t think  the United States is going to slow down.” So they have a healthy degree of cynicism there.  Now, obviously there’s a degree of performance in   that — they’re performing for a certain kind of  American audience. But on that point at least,   I think that’s a credible position  that likely many of them do believe. Tom Reed: I also want to understand a bit more  how the CCP might respond to blisteringly fast   AI progress, if it does happen. I’d like to  know: is there anything that exists within   Xi Jinping Thought that would make sense of a  potential tenfold acceleration of scientific   and technological progress? What concepts  does he have available to make sense of this? Julian Gewirtz: It’s a really interesting  way of putting the question. When we think   about speed of progress and development,  there are few societies on earth that have   dealt with that dynamic as recently as China  itself. Meaning if you think of China in 1980,   and if you think of China today in 2026, that is  a stunning speed of transformation. And that’s not   a tenfold increase in tech progress in the span  of a year — we can talk about those kind of hard   takeoff scenarios — but it is, by the standards of  pretty much all human history, pretty darn fast. So I say that because when we compare  it to societies that have been wealthy   and experienced sort of development in  a more gradual process or longer ago,   I just think there is something  interesting there in that   fact that China has experienced such  rapid development in the recent past. But I don’t think any of that prepares any of us,  in either country or anywhere around the world,   for that kind of speed. And I think  in the minds of Chinese leaders,   the risk of losing control over these systems,  over society, over technology, is a risk that   kind of has a much deeper and more fundamental  status than it does even in the United States. Because if you think about the way in which, in  Xi Jinping’s kind of more ideological thinking,   technology is positioned, it is,  as he says, the main battlefield   of international competition. But it is  also kind of a physical instantiation of   political power. And the Chinese Communist  Party’s relationship to technology over a   long time has been that this is something  we need to harness to drive the development   of China — the so-called great rejuvenation of  China — and our political power more generally. In the 1980s, when the information  revolution started to happen,   Chinese leaders were thinking about very  rapid — by those standards — shifts,   and wanting not to miss out on them, as they  had missed out, in their telling, on the prior— Tom Reed: The Industrial Revolution. Julian Gewirtz: Exactly. Obviously  missed out on the Industrial Revolution,   and missed out on several prior waves.  Xi Jinping has said this revolution,   we will not just not miss out  on, but we will help lead. So those are some of the concerns and  considerations that would be a part of   this. But I also will just maybe end  this answer by saying the question of   kind of exactly how this plays out, and  exactly how much control by that point   the Communist Party thinks it has, is  going to shape so much of this. Because,   for instance, right now Beijing is still  significantly constrained on compute.   They see themselves as behind, relentlessly  trying to catch up. But if, by whatever point   we’re talking about in this hypothetical, they  feel less constrained on compute — which I don’t   think is terribly likely, but let’s say —  or they feel that they have reached closer   to parity at the frontier and suddenly it  might be slipping out of their grasp, I think   those are just profound uncertainties that could  introduce even more volatility into this moment. Tom Reed: And we just don’t know. Julian Gewirtz: I hate to kind  of have a fancy four-part answer,   the upshot of which is that we don’t know  — but it’s the truth. And maybe just more   generally to say, as we think about why this is  so challenging for the Chinese Communist Party:   this is generally a system  that moves pretty slowly. There are exceptions to that, and I think  AI governance could end up being one of the   exceptions to that. But they move pretty  slowly. They like to have these really   laborious deliberative processes, paper and  endless meetings and all of that. And they,   like pretty much any government — but to a pretty  intense extreme, given the authoritarian nature   of the system — want certainty. And so in  their system, one of the hardest things— Tom Reed: Good luck with that. Julian Gewirtz: Exactly. One of the hardest  things about frontier risk has been that the   upshot of every conversation is, “We don’t know,  but the scale of outcomes is near infinite.” Tom Reed: Who actually has shaped the CCP’s  views on AI the most? I remember you have   this great article from a couple of years ago  about the influence of the American futurist   Alvin Toffler on China’s sort of national  R&D programme in the sort of late 1980s.   They read a lot of Alvin Toffler, and apparently  this inspired a lot of their approach to using   new information technologies. Who might  be the equivalents for AI? Who are they   reading to understand what this technology  is about and what opportunities it offers? Julian Gewirtz: Well, there are a few ways to  get at that question. One is that, for good or   for ill, a lot of people in that system, I  think, are reading a lot of the same stuff   that Americans read — meaning the core people  who are working in the labs, in the companies,   generally have had exposure, even if they haven’t  studied in the United States. It’s a pretty global   research ecosystem — increasingly, I think,  less that way, but there is that there. And we do see people in the Chinese  ecosystem respond to everybody from   Dario to Leopold Aschenbrenner and whoever else. Tom Reed: This is at the labs? Julian Gewirtz: Yeah, this is at the  labs. But I think that’s important,   because one of the really interesting dynamics  inside China is that the companies — or some   of the companies — I think have very  different visions of the AI future than   the Chinese Communist Party. And so that  was where I was kind of going with this,   which is that there has been a debate, for  instance, about whether China — air quotes around   “China” — is AGI-pilled. And I think the candid  way to answer that is many of the labs are. The   Chinese government has been much less oriented  that way, but I think even that is changing. And I think the upshot is that now, basically,  the views that are shaping the Chinese Communist   Party on this are increasingly internal to the  Chinese Communist Party. They are not publishing   essays on microsites. They are reporting up  through the system. And one of the reasons   that I think more engagement, technical exchange,  and dialogue is a good thing between these two   countries is we need to be really thinking  about how we’re shaping those reports that   go up to the top Chinese leaders that they pick  up and read. Because what’s in there is likely   very different than what Liang Wenfeng, the  DeepSeek CEO, might say on an investor call. Tom Reed: In a world where Xi does end  up taking the idea seriously that AI   could lead to something like a tenfold  acceleration in scientific progress,   how would that have happened? Who would  be the sort of important precursors to   Xi also believing this? Do we know what the  information flow could plausibly look like? Julian Gewirtz: It’s a really  interesting question to unpack,   and I don’t want to get way too in  the weeds on this, but basically, we— Tom Reed: Get an org chart out. Julian Gewirtz: No, exactly. You can  put it up on the screen. But basically,   their responsibility on AI is somewhat diffused  across different parts of the Chinese government,   because the fundamental approach that they have  taken to AI policy — not AI safety, but just   AI policy more generally — the shorthand is AI  Plus: essentially integrating AI into everything. Of course, they have made tremendous progress  integrating it into manufacturing and robotics.   They are integrating it into the military.  They’re integrating it into the political and   state security apparatus, and so on. So that means  that responsibility is somewhat differentiated. I think the least likely way  that Xi Jinping comes to that   impression is that he reads a bunch  of essays from American lab leaders. Tom Reed: What would be a more likely route?   Maybe if it comes from the industry  themselves, perhaps, or it’s unclear? Julian Gewirtz: I mean, I think the likeliest  route, honestly, is that it starts to happen in   the United States first, and it doesn’t feel like  it’s happening in China. And the effect is that,   in connection to their becoming more  concerned about the risks domestically,   they also see the possibility of the United  States really pulling ahead very quickly. And I think that’s a moment when you can  have very divergent paths. But there’s   a nonzero chance of a path — if the United  States is smart about how it approaches it,   which I think is a big if — where you could  imagine Beijing coming to some sort of internal   reckoning that pacing is clearly in their  interest. Small probability, but nonzero. Tom Reed: Is there anyone important in  China who might have what we would call   the Silicon Valley view of AI? Do you think  there’s anyone other than perhaps the lab   leaders themselves? So we kind of have to have both strategies  firing on all cylinders at once. And then just again, the third thing that I’d  say is we also have to be tracking so closely   how Beijing sees these risks, because as their own  risk perception evolves, there will be windows of   opportunity. And I don’t know that necessarily  the current team is thinking about it this way,   but certainly if I were in government,  or if others who have this approach were,   I think you’d be looking for these windows,  these moments when Beijing starts to take the   risk more seriously, and seeing those  as each creating an opening — not for   a sweeping grand bargain that solves all of  our problems overnight, but for incremental   progress that gets us to a better place on a  timescale that’s relevant, but also realistic. Tom Reed: What is the right level of pessimism to   have about the prospect of China as an  international partner? As I understand,   in 2023 there was a US offer of something  like a nuclear crisis hotline, which they   stonewalled or rejected. They also didn’t really  exchange timely information with the rest of the   world on COVID. What’s the right way to view  how cooperative they’re likely to be or not? Julian Gewirtz: I think probably it’s come  across through this conversation that I   think we have to have a pretty limited  sense of what they’re going to see as in   their interest — to return to that core idea.  It’s never going to be a binary switch where   they go from seeing this as this intense  domain of competition to suddenly seeing   this as a no-brainer: “Any rational person  would understand, we gotta make a deal.” So I think that initial point that I made  — about we gotta begin from China as it is,   and how they think about these challenges, rather  than how we think they ought to — is core there. I will say that in some of those areas  you alluded to, like nuclear arms control,   there is a similarity, in  the fact that they’re behind,   or they have fewer nuclear weapons.  And they therefore always say,   “Why would you talk about constraints with  us when you have so many more than we do?” The other thing I would say,  which I probably should have said   earlier, but better late than never, is they  often, I think, over the past couple decades,   have looked at the United States and felt that we  get certain fundamental risk factors wrong. They   looked at the global financial crisis in 2008,  and they said the United States fundamentally got   wrong the financial risk in its own system,  on the side of way too much risk tolerance. They look at the predictions that were  made 25 years ago about how the internet   was going to change China. Remember, 25  years ago, Bill Clinton said that trying   to control the internet was like trying to  nail Jell-O to the wall. He literally said   “good luck” to China. And they were staring  down those predictions, and they said, “No,   the United States is wrong. We are going  to nail Jell-O to the wall.” And they did. Tom Reed: And how do you keep your ambition?  Because when I think about, sometimes, all of   the things that a real full deal on AI might  require, we’re talking about potentially many   years of not just monitoring each other’s compute  supply chains, but also monitoring each other’s   robotics supply chains. We’re talking about what  might need to be a completely unprecedented level   of cooperation between these two countries, on  a technology for which there is less consensus   about the risks, on a technology that is  moving faster than any previous technology.   Sometimes I just think it seems completely  impossible. How do you view our chances here? Julian Gewirtz: Well, I guess the way that I  think about it is, rather than designing in the   abstract a mental model of what the ideal deal  would look like — I think if you’re doing that,   if you’re doing the kind of AI 2040 thing, the  impossibility confronts you at every turn. But   in fact, I don’t think right now that kind  of ideal mechanism design is the most urgent   question. I think figuring out how we  can start immediately, wasting no time,   to take incremental steps in the right  direction, based on an understanding of each   of our self-interests, is the question  before us — the most urgent problem. Tom Reed: And that’s tractable. Julian Gewirtz: And that is tractable. So I think  beginning there, and then also continually saying:   what is actually happening in the technological  development? What are the scope of predictions   or models for how this goes? Where is the  discourse in China? Where is the discourse   in the United States? And trying to just, again,  be continually ambitious and opportunistic about   it. I think that, as a mental model, shall we  say — in addition to just a praxis — that is   actually not such a dark place to be, even though  it’s still an alarming and challenging moment. the hardest version of the question right now is  if someone were to ask me, “What does success look   like in a year?” And I say that’s the hardest  version because, as you know better than I do,   you have RSI timelines that are shorter than that.  You have just such fundamental uncertainty about   the technology itself, in addition to the  geopolitics and everything else. So to me,   it’s the kind of classic one foot in  front of the other, walk before you run. Tom Reed: What’s the phrase about stepping,  making your way over the river, over the stones? Julian Gewirtz: Right, exactly.  There’s a famous Chinese saying,   which Deng Xiaoping used about economic reform:  crossing the river by feeling for the stones.   I don’t see another alternative, because  we’re not gonna sit down at a table and   design a perfect mechanism and  then implement it tomorrow. Tom Reed: I now have a series of very selfish  questions I would like to ask you, in that I’m   essentially interested in how I could build or  recognise real China expertise. In particular,   I’m wondering: how do you recognise  a China specialist as the real deal   when the whole field is really quite opaque? Julian Gewirtz: So the number one thing is  humility. If a China expert comes to me, or comes   to anybody, and says they have all the answers  and are presenting them with total confidence,   the bullshit metre should go off  right away. And from my perspective,   the central challenge of doing China  policy and building China expertise really   is dealing with uncertainty and having  nonetheless to make educated decisions. That’s square one. Some of that has come  across in this conversation, I hope,   where we’re sort of saying there are some things  we know, there are some things we don’t know,   and everything we’re trying to  do is in that space between them. And then second, it’s not easy to go spend  time in China, necessarily, for everybody. But   people who have spent time there, who have a  long track record, who read the source material   and have the context to make sense of it —  that’s also just essential, and it’s hard. It’s this funny thing I feel at this point in  my career: I am doing that almost every day,   and I was doing that almost every day a  decade ago. And it has not gotten more fun,   because Chinese Communist Party documents are not  beautiful New Yorker articles written to keep the   reader interested, and certainly aren’t in  short-form video. But candidly, there’s no   other way. And it’s how that system works. And so  if you want to understand it, you gotta go there. Tom Reed: Where in China should I hang out?  I’ve been to Beijing, I’ve been to Shanghai,   I’ve been to Hangzhou, I went to WAIC [World  Artificial Intelligence Conference] this   summer. But other than that— I mean,  I also don’t speak Mandarin. But if   you were to recommend to me, “You  should really go to these cities”— Julian Gewirtz: Well, hold on. I was giving you   an answer to how a hardcore  China expert should operate.   I think there is a different answer for somebody  who wants to be educated and informed on China,   but is not going to make their professional life  being the China expert in the room, so to speak. So for that category — which, unless  you’re planning a major life renovation,   I feel like is probably the sweet spot — I  don’t think actually you need to be going   and... There’s a famous Sinologist who  described reading these Chinese Communist   Party documents as eating sawdust. So I  don’t think you need to be doing that. But yeah, I think getting over  there, getting exposure directly,   and then also finding a staple of things  you read and people you talk with who are   really reliable — and who are not making  BS calls, but are kind of really doing   the hard work as intermediaries, almost —  that’s sort of the most essential thing. And then I also think remembering that China is  not simply the Chinese Communist Party, and there   is incredible cultural production, and there’s  actually a really diverse kind of ecosystem. And some of the most interesting moments  over the past few years for me have been   when friends of mine... For instance, a  lot of people who are on TikTok migrated   briefly to a Chinese app when TikTok  went offline here in the United States,   and were coming to me, sending me videos of  people in China singing and doing all kinds of   random stuff. And it was sort of like, wow, this  is actually a degree of exposure to China that   friends of mine who have nothing to  do with China are suddenly getting. In terms of where to go in China, for most  foreigners who travel there, you hit the   kind of main tech-focused hubs — Shanghai and  Hangzhou — and then Beijing, which is one of the   old imperial capitals and today the place where  the Chinese Communist Party is headquartered.   It’s a huge country with a lot of diversity,  geographically and all that. So I do think   it’s always good to kind of get out of the main  coastal hubs, where you see all the development   and all the modernity, and get to places that  are a little bit more off the beaten path. But I’ll also just be candid and say  that’s hard to do as a foreigner,   particularly somebody who doesn’t speak  Chinese. So I think you don’t have to   set too high a bar for yourself. If you make  it to Beijing and Shanghai, you are already   in the very top percentage of people in the  West who have exposure directly to China. Tom Reed: I will say, I was surprised at how much  heavy lifting Google Translate could do for me,   though. It’s a very well-oiled machine,  where people know to pull out their   translation apps. You can usually  get across the things you need to. Julian Gewirtz: Yeah, not to tie this  back to the substance of our conversation,   but that does actually reflect, I think,  a really interesting difference that we   observe between the United States and China,  which is just a much higher degree of comfort   with and optimism about AI over there  than here in the United States. The   polling is remarkable on this. Basically,  the United States is at the very bottom of   rankings for optimism about the benefits of  AI for people, and China is at the very top. And what you just said made me think of  it, because it’s exactly that thing of:   you’re walking around Beijing or Shanghai,   and someone in China whose life is already  largely integrated on WeChat and into   other virtual platforms is very comfortable  doing a bit of real-time speech translation,   and having that be kind of seamless, in a way  that I think is still pretty unusual here. Tom Reed: Yeah. OK, you’re not going to like  this next question, because I’m going to ask   you not to be humble, and you just told me  that the mark of a China expert is humility.   But what is the nature of your edge? What do  you think is the thing you understand about   China better than almost anyone else in the  US? Is there a thing you would identify there? Julian Gewirtz: OK, that is making  me uncomfortable. So, I mean,   I don’t think this is a unique-to-me thing, but  I do think the most important kind of skill that   I have tried to acquire is not simply to  treat China policy as some sequestered,   distant, esoteric thing that happens over  there — and then you bring back the right   answer to people who care about domestic policy   or broader US foreign policy or tech policy — but  to see it as totally integrated and inextricable. And that’s actually, I find, very challenging  intellectually, because you have to master the   China side of it. You have to do all that deep  work — getting your PhD in modern Chinese history   or politics or whatever the case may be, spending  time there, learning how the system works. And   then you have to somehow then also figure out how  to make that integrated into the tradeoffs that   policymakers and business leaders have  to make when it comes to China policy. Because one of the themes, in a way, of what  we’ve been discussing is there might be an   ideal set of solutions vis-à-vis China, but at  every turn reality presses against them in some   way. And I think in the field of people who work  on this stuff, that skill, when I have seen it,   is the most impressive thing, and I’m  trying to bring it to bear in my own career. Tom Reed: Who else should I be  reading, other than your blog,   Paper Tiger? Are there other things  which you would really recommend to me? Julian Gewirtz: A lot of things. When I  was in government I did a lot of work on   US–China tech competition, and before I  went into government I was writing about   Chinese technology policy a lot. But what I  saw over the four years I worked in the Biden   administration made me convinced that the AI  story that we’ve been talking about today was   on a scale of importance so much greater than  almost anything else I could imagine doing. So when I came out, I was like, “I’m going  to use the time that I now find myself with   to go as deep as I can.” And I talked  to a few friends who were those people,   and were much deeper, and basically  got a reading list from them. So I learned so much from Matt Sheehan, who we  mentioned; from Graham Webster, who’s out at   Stanford and does incredible work; from colleagues  at CSET, the Center for Security and Emerging   Technology — people I’m sure are well known  to your listeners, like Helen Toner; and from   Chris McGuire, who’s at the Council on Foreign  Relations now, and many others on the AI account. But I would just say, to me, one of  the most striking things is these are   not all people who agree on the policy solutions,   but they are all people who are doing the really  hard work analytically, and who sort of share   that with the public in a really meaningful  way. So that’s sort of on the AI account. And then on China, I mean,  we are in a little-noticed   sort of renaissance or flowering of amazing  China studies and China scholarship. And I   say little-noticed because I think there’s a meme  out there that, because it has gotten harder to   go to China and do research, the quality of  China studies must therefore have suffered. And one of the most extraordinary things  to me is that, despite how hard it is,   there is incredible work happening in the  academy and think tanks and elsewhere, and   journalism — even though for the journalists it’s  incredibly hard; many of them can’t even go to   China anymore. So I think my diet of China-related  content feels as rich as it’s ever been. And just there, I would say, maybe for your  listeners — they can like to nerd out; obviously   they’re certainly doing that if they’ve reached  this point in our conversation. And so there,   I would say it’s worth actually reading  some of the stuff that China academics   are doing — not just the people who are  sort of in the hot-take industry, but-- Tom Reed: My industry. [laughs] Julian Gewirtz: Well, no, I mean, I don’t  think that’s fair. But there’s a book that   I always give as an example of this for me,  which is an academic book called The Gilded   Cage by a Harvard sociologist named Ya-Wen Lei.  She has a whole framework for the development of   China’s technology regulatory regime. And it’s a  classic example of extraordinary scholarly work   that actually has direct relevance to the  kinds of things we have been talking about   every day. But you’re not going to know  about it unless you are in this field. Tom Reed: What’s it about? The  Gilded Cage? What’s it about? Julian Gewirtz: It’s basically about the  development of China’s technology regulatory   regime for the internet and for fintech. And  she did an incredible amount of fieldwork   embedded in tech companies in China, and  she also comes up with a series of kind   of frameworks for analysing this.  And she’s playing for 2big stakes:   she’s playing for fundamental understandings  about development and state capitalism in China,   relations of firms and the state. But it’s  just a good example of this kind of book. And there are some books that cross over,  like Joseph Torigian’s biography of Xi   Jinping’s father, which is a deep scholarly  work crossed over, got broader attention. Tom Reed: This is The Party Comes First? Julian Gewirtz: Exactly. And I always think  about the fact that, for each of those books,   there are two or three others that maybe don’t,  but have a huge amount to offer as well. And so   one of the things I’m trying to do, actually,  in my own writing is, as much as I can,   give a little lift to some of those works --  because they’re out there; it’s happening.   China studies is vibrant in all of these ways,  and yeah, it’s a cool moment to be in the field. Tom Reed: Great. Do you have a favourite  non-dissident Chinese intellectual? Julian Gewirtz: The people who I find most  interesting are largely not people I agree   with. It’s not like I’m reading Chinese academics  and nodding along saying, “Preach,” or whatever. But for instance, there’s a guy named Jiang  Shigong — and I can send you some stuff of   his — but he is very far from somebody  who I think shares any views with me,   but I find him to be an enormously revealing  analyst of contemporary China, of Xi Jinping.   And he’s a very ambitious intellectual. He  is very supportive of many of the things Xi   Jinping does, and he’s definitely comfortably  operating, by all accounts, in that system. But when I think about who has been  the most sort of precise framework   generator that has helped me generate my own  frameworks for understanding that system,   his work is quite useful, and a bunch of it has  been translated — even if I’m like, “I do not   like the upshot of that for America.” But it’s  important to actually reckon with those people. And I would say, more generally, there is a  set of government-aligned thinkers who are   serious thinkers. These are not simply  people who are doing propaganda work,   but they are very supportive of what China is  doing. And I think it’s actually really important   for people in my position to read them, to  reckon with them, to take their ideas seriously. The best example of this, by the way, is  Wang Huning, who we mentioned earlier,   who’s one of Xi Jinping’s top advisers. He’s on  the Politburo Standing Committee. He started off   as [an international politics] professor at  Fudan University, and a number of his early   writings — all the way back from the 1980s and  early 1990s — are still incredibly interesting,   layered reads, and sometimes they get caricatured. His most famous book is called America Against  America, and it sometimes is described as just   an anti-America polemic. And there’s a lot  of criticism of the United States in there,   for sure, but there’s also all this really  interesting language about how technologically   advanced the United States is and how innovative  the United States is. And when you think about how   he has approached governing China, actually  both sides of that are really important. And a closer reading of that text —  a closer understanding of this isn’t   only the parts that are about what  he sees in America and criticises,   but also what he sees in America and envies  -- both of those impulses shape what he and   Xi Jinping and other Chinese leaders have  done. So yeah, it’s important to reckon with. Tom Reed: What Chinese intellectual  currents that are particularly relevant   to AI policy do you think we should be  aware of? So I’m vaguely familiar with   the Industrial Party as a movement. I’ve read  Lu Nanfeng and Wu Jing’s essay on this. Can   you carve them into blocks that I should  reckon with, or is that difficult to do? Julian Gewirtz: So I’d say a couple things.  First, there is a longstanding sort of futurist   strand of writing in China. You mentioned earlier  in our conversation the Alvin Toffler influence   in the 1980s that I wrote about. And I think  understanding these kind of techno-futurist   visions in China, and the way in which they see  industrial development and party leadership,   is one really important strand of thinking. A second, which used to be much buzzier a few  years ago and has certainly diminished since then,   is Chinese science fiction. Jordan Schneider,   who does the ChinaTalk podcast and is a  friend, likes to talk about how influential   sci-fi has been in shaping American  and Western visions of the AGI future. And there was this incredible flowering  of science fiction writing in China   over the course of the 1980s, 1990s,  and 2000s. And it was one of those   areas where you saw people doing  politically sensitive writing,   but somehow getting away with it under the sort  of sci-fi banner. And I think it’s important for   people who are trying to understand the kind  of currents in China to look at that writing. And obviously Liu Cixin is the most famous — The  Three-Body Problem is the most famous — but there   are a range of others. There’s a guy named Chen  Qiufan, who ended up actually cowriting a book   with Kai-Fu Lee on AI futures, but is also just  a really interesting sci-fi writer; a woman named   Hao Jingfang, who wrote an amazing sort of novella  — long short story — about kind of inequality   in Beijing. And so there’s a number of these  things which are really interesting, even if the   space for that writing is smaller now. But I think  it reflects this kind of set of possibilities. And then, I guess, third and  finally, just to kind of foreground,   is to say: reading these regime-aligned or  regime-supportive intellectuals in China,   who position AI at the absolute heart of the way  in which power will be distributed in the future,   and give that kind of deeper intellectual  foundation to Xi Jinping saying something   like “technology is the main battlefield of  international competition” — that’s really   important too, in addition to reading the  people who are actually working on AI issues. Tom Reed: And what about using the AI models   themselves? Which AI model  is the best China watcher? Julian Gewirtz: Of the Chinese models? Tom Reed: Across the whole range. If  you’re doing research with a model,   which one are you using? I’ve found, for instance,   ChatGPT seems to be better at finding WeChat  links than Claude, for whatever reason. Julian Gewirtz: Yeah, it’s interesting you said  that. I was about to say something similar,   which is, I’m not terribly original on this, but  yeah, I find for the kind of research that I’m   doing — to the extent that I’m using AI to help  me do it — ChatGPT somehow has seemingly greater   facility with the Chinese parts of the internet  than Claude. And I’ve heard some people say I   should be checking out Gemini more on this front.  I confess that I haven’t really. To the extent   that I’m using this, I’m pretty satisfied with  what I’m getting. But yeah, it is interesting. And I will say, for me, what I have not done,  but others have done — and there’s some really   interesting work on this — is kind of comparing  what you find when you research China on Chinese   models and American models. Obviously we all  know about certain censorship guardrails that   are built in. It’s not surprising that you  find much less about the Tiananmen crackdown   on a Chinese model, but that, actually, because  of the priority given to the training corpus   being in Chinese, there are sometimes  very different answers you get when you   ask the question in Chinese versus in English  — which is itself a really interesting thing,   and I suspect is also probably true  in some of the American models. But that connection between the corpus  that’s being used — the language of the   corpus that’s being used to train — and  the kind of epistemic consequences of   that is something that I think is just  going to become more and more important. By the way, we are beginning to see  a Chinese discourse on this too:   people in China writing about the fact  that what they choose to feed in is what   others will be processing for centuries to  come — and hoping to shape international   discourse through shaping the kind of corpus  of Chinese and China-relevant material — is   a super interesting area that there’s  some work happening on, and we need more. Tom Reed: Do we have any idea what  they’d be prioritising other than   censorship? What narratives would  they be actively trying to push? Julian Gewirtz: Absolutely. So the simplest  version is essentially propaganda, where the   goal is to push a positive set of narratives  about China and downplay criticisms of China;   a positive set of narratives about Chinese  leaders, downplay criticism of them. But then   there’s a whole range of other topics, like  Taiwan -- where their goal is to maximally   shape a version of understanding of Taiwan  issues that comports with their official line. And the idea that we could have models that  would be unwittingly built in such a way that   they reinforce that, I think, is the kind  of concern that is really reasonable to   have — particularly now that we begin to  see corners of the sort of official and   semi-official discourse in China talking  about this as an opportunity for them. Tom Reed: A final question I have: where do you  think are the best places on Earth to visit to   understand China’s international strategy  and its investment in the Global South? Julian Gewirtz: I spent a bit of time when I  was at the State Department working on this   issue set and doing a lot of travel around it. To focus on the Global South questions  specifically, my own view is that it’s   good to get a kind of spectrum of different  places that have found different ways,   and are finding different ways, of striking  the balance between getting more benefit out   of their ties with China and maintaining their  own sovereignty and autonomy on the world stage. So at one end of that spectrum  you have India — a country that,   because of the border conflict and other issues,  decided to block a bunch of Chinese apps,   and really try to push back against Chinese  influence. And I think it’s super interesting   and important to hear their perspective, which is  not one-for-one with the Washington perspective,   even though it is quite concerned  about increasing Chinese influence. Then I think Central Asia is a super interesting  place, because of the dynamic of competition   between China and Russia there. Obviously China  and Russia are close strategic partners, but they   also have some areas where they’re competing  for influence, and Central Asia is one of them. Another super interesting place, which I have  not been to, but I think would love to sort of   see and talk to people on this score, is Egypt —  where Xi Jinping just went on a state visit — and   the kind of question there of a country that  has deep security ties with the United States,   but is clearly making a major play to upgrade  its relationship with China. Super interesting. And then in the Western Hemisphere, I  also think — whether it’s Mexico, where   there has been a tonne of scale-up of Chinese  companies manufacturing, or Peru, where China   has been building this megaport on the Pacific  coast — these are really significant stories. And then finally, I would just say: every  year, the first trip abroad that the Chinese   foreign minister takes, for decades, has been to  Africa. And it is a place where China, I think,   has a much more complex and differentiated  and layered strategy than some accounts   would have you think. But whether you’re going  to countries that have really gone all in and   see the Chinese development model as something  that they want to ride for their own development,   or to countries that feel like they’ve  gotten bad deals out of China but still   know that they have to have a good relationship  with Beijing — super worthwhile. I realise I   have just essentially told you to go to  every place in the world, but the upshot— Tom Reed: I like an excuse to go everywhere. Julian Gewirtz: Exactly, exactly. You should  get the podcast to pay for it. But no,   I guess to my mind, the upshot of all of that is:  China has a global strategy. It is pursuing it in   many different ways around the world. It wants  global influence. It wants that influence to   look different than American global influence has  looked. But there’s no one place where you can go   to see it all, because Beijing is doing so many  different things in so many different places. Tom Reed: Great. Well, it’s been a real pleasure,   Julian. Thank you for coming on the  show, and talk to you next time.
