Tom Reed: Great. Do you have a favourite  non-dissident Chinese intellectual?
Julian Gewirtz: The people who I find most  interesting are largely not people I agree
with. It’s not like I’m reading Chinese academics  and nodding along saying, “Preach,” or whatever.
But for instance, there’s a guy named Jiang  Shigong — and I can send you some stuff of
his — but he is very far from somebody  who I think shares any views with me,
but I find him to be an enormously revealing  analyst of contemporary China, of Xi Jinping.
And he’s a very ambitious intellectual. He  is very supportive of many of the things Xi
Jinping does, and he’s definitely comfortably  operating, by all accounts, in that system.
But when I think about who has been  the most sort of precise framework
generator that has helped me generate my own  frameworks for understanding that system,
his work is quite useful, and a bunch of it has  been translated — even if I’m like, “I do not
like the upshot of that for America.” But it’s  important to actually reckon with those people.
And I would say, more generally, there is a  set of government-aligned thinkers who are
serious thinkers. These are not simply  people who are doing propaganda work,
but they are very supportive of what China is  doing. And I think it’s actually really important
for people in my position to read them, to  reckon with them, to take their ideas seriously.
The best example of this, by the way, is  Wang Huning, who we mentioned earlier,
who’s one of Xi Jinping’s top advisers. He’s on  the Politburo Standing Committee. He started off
as [an international politics] professor at  Fudan University, and a number of his early
writings — all the way back from the 1980s and  early 1990s — are still incredibly interesting,
layered reads, and sometimes they get caricatured.
His most famous book is called America Against  America, and it sometimes is described as just
an anti-America polemic. And there’s a lot  of criticism of the United States in there,
for sure, but there’s also all this really  interesting language about how technologically
advanced the United States is and how innovative  the United States is. And when you think about how
he has approached governing China, actually  both sides of that are really important.
And a closer reading of that text —  a closer understanding of this isn’t
only the parts that are about what  he sees in America and criticises,
but also what he sees in America and envies  -- both of those impulses shape what he and
Xi Jinping and other Chinese leaders have  done. So yeah, it’s important to reckon with.
Tom Reed: What Chinese intellectual  currents that are particularly relevant
to AI policy do you think we should be  aware of? So I’m vaguely familiar with
the Industrial Party as a movement. I’ve read  Lu Nanfeng and Wu Jing’s essay on this. Can
you carve them into blocks that I should  reckon with, or is that difficult to do?
Julian Gewirtz: So I’d say a couple things.  First, there is a longstanding sort of futurist
strand of writing in China. You mentioned earlier  in our conversation the Alvin Toffler influence
in the 1980s that I wrote about. And I think  understanding these kind of techno-futurist
visions in China, and the way in which they see  industrial development and party leadership,
is one really important strand of thinking.
A second, which used to be much buzzier a few  years ago and has certainly diminished since then,
is Chinese science fiction. Jordan Schneider,
who does the ChinaTalk podcast and is a  friend, likes to talk about how influential
sci-fi has been in shaping American  and Western visions of the AGI future.
And there was this incredible flowering  of science fiction writing in China
over the course of the 1980s, 1990s,  and 2000s. And it was one of those
areas where you saw people doing  politically sensitive writing,
but somehow getting away with it under the sort  of sci-fi banner. And I think it’s important for
people who are trying to understand the kind  of currents in China to look at that writing.
And obviously Liu Cixin is the most famous — The  Three-Body Problem is the most famous — but there
are a range of others. There’s a guy named Chen  Qiufan, who ended up actually cowriting a book
with Kai-Fu Lee on AI futures, but is also just  a really interesting sci-fi writer; a woman named
Hao Jingfang, who wrote an amazing sort of novella  — long short story — about kind of inequality
in Beijing. And so there’s a number of these  things which are really interesting, even if the
space for that writing is smaller now. But I think  it reflects this kind of set of possibilities.
And then, I guess, third and  finally, just to kind of foreground,
is to say: reading these regime-aligned or  regime-supportive intellectuals in China,
who position AI at the absolute heart of the way  in which power will be distributed in the future,
and give that kind of deeper intellectual  foundation to Xi Jinping saying something
like “technology is the main battlefield of  international competition” — that’s really
important too, in addition to reading the  people who are actually working on AI issues.
Tom Reed: And what about using the AI models
themselves? Which AI model  is the best China watcher?
Julian Gewirtz: Of the Chinese models?
Tom Reed: Across the whole range. If  you’re doing research with a model,
which one are you using? I’ve found, for instance,
ChatGPT seems to be better at finding WeChat  links than Claude, for whatever reason.
Julian Gewirtz: Yeah, it’s interesting you said  that. I was about to say something similar,
which is, I’m not terribly original on this, but  yeah, I find for the kind of research that I’m
doing — to the extent that I’m using AI to help  me do it — ChatGPT somehow has seemingly greater
facility with the Chinese parts of the internet  than Claude. And I’ve heard some people say I
should be checking out Gemini more on this front.  I confess that I haven’t really. To the extent
that I’m using this, I’m pretty satisfied with  what I’m getting. But yeah, it is interesting.
And I will say, for me, what I have not done,  but others have done — and there’s some really
interesting work on this — is kind of comparing  what you find when you research China on Chinese
models and American models. Obviously we all  know about certain censorship guardrails that
are built in. It’s not surprising that you  find much less about the Tiananmen crackdown
on a Chinese model, but that, actually, because  of the priority given to the training corpus
being in Chinese, there are sometimes  very different answers you get when you
ask the question in Chinese versus in English  — which is itself a really interesting thing,
and I suspect is also probably true  in some of the American models.
But that connection between the corpus  that’s being used — the language of the
corpus that’s being used to train — and  the kind of epistemic consequences of
that is something that I think is just  going to become more and more important.
By the way, we are beginning to see  a Chinese discourse on this too:
people in China writing about the fact  that what they choose to feed in is what
others will be processing for centuries to  come — and hoping to shape international
discourse through shaping the kind of corpus  of Chinese and China-relevant material — is
a super interesting area that there’s  some work happening on, and we need more.
Tom Reed: Do we have any idea what  they’d be prioritising other than
censorship? What narratives would  they be actively trying to push?
Julian Gewirtz: Absolutely. So the simplest  version is essentially propaganda, where the
goal is to push a positive set of narratives  about China and downplay criticisms of China;
a positive set of narratives about Chinese  leaders, downplay criticism of them. But then
there’s a whole range of other topics, like  Taiwan -- where their goal is to maximally
shape a version of understanding of Taiwan  issues that comports with their official line.
And the idea that we could have models that  would be unwittingly built in such a way that
they reinforce that, I think, is the kind  of concern that is really reasonable to
have — particularly now that we begin to  see corners of the sort of official and
semi-official discourse in China talking  about this as an opportunity for them.
Tom Reed: A final question I have: where do you  think are the best places on Earth to visit to
understand China’s international strategy  and its investment in the Global South?
Julian Gewirtz: I spent a bit of time when I  was at the State Department working on this
issue set and doing a lot of travel around it.
To focus on the Global South questions  specifically, my own view is that it’s
good to get a kind of spectrum of different  places that have found different ways,
and are finding different ways, of striking  the balance between getting more benefit out
of their ties with China and maintaining their  own sovereignty and autonomy on the world stage.
So at one end of that spectrum  you have India — a country that,
because of the border conflict and other issues,  decided to block a bunch of Chinese apps,
and really try to push back against Chinese  influence. And I think it’s super interesting
and important to hear their perspective, which is  not one-for-one with the Washington perspective,
even though it is quite concerned  about increasing Chinese influence.
Then I think Central Asia is a super interesting  place, because of the dynamic of competition
between China and Russia there. Obviously China  and Russia are close strategic partners, but they
also have some areas where they’re competing  for influence, and Central Asia is one of them.
Another super interesting place, which I have  not been to, but I think would love to sort of
see and talk to people on this score, is Egypt —  where Xi Jinping just went on a state visit — and
the kind of question there of a country that  has deep security ties with the United States,
but is clearly making a major play to upgrade  its relationship with China. Super interesting.
And then in the Western Hemisphere, I  also think — whether it’s Mexico, where
there has been a tonne of scale-up of Chinese  companies manufacturing, or Peru, where China
has been building this megaport on the Pacific  coast — these are really significant stories.
And then finally, I would just say: every  year, the first trip abroad that the Chinese
foreign minister takes, for decades, has been to  Africa. And it is a place where China, I think,
has a much more complex and differentiated  and layered strategy than some accounts
would have you think. But whether you’re going  to countries that have really gone all in and
see the Chinese development model as something  that they want to ride for their own development,
or to countries that feel like they’ve  gotten bad deals out of China but still
know that they have to have a good relationship  with Beijing — super worthwhile. I realise I
have just essentially told you to go to  every place in the world, but the upshot—
Tom Reed: I like an excuse to go everywhere.
Julian Gewirtz: Exactly, exactly. You should  get the podcast to pay for it. But no,
I guess to my mind, the upshot of all of that is:  China has a global strategy. It is pursuing it in
many different ways around the world. It wants  global influence. It wants that influence to
look different than American global influence has  looked. But there’s no one place where you can go
to see it all, because Beijing is doing so many  different things in so many different places.
Tom Reed: Great. Well, it’s been a real pleasure,
Julian. Thank you for coming on the  show, and talk to you next time.
